threads.thread_goal: Align on campaign objectives, target segments, and value proposition

messages.text: Hi team, I've drafted the initial campaign strategy brief (A1) and wanted to get your feedback before we lock in direction. The core idea is positioning our printed catalog service as a premium, customizable solution for B2B companies looking to stand out. I've outlined three potential target segments: e-commerce brands, industrial suppliers, and professional services firms. Primary value prop: 'Catalogs that convert—personalized, print-quality, delivered fast.' Secondary: cost-per-unit efficiency at scale. Objectives are to drive 150 qualified leads in the first 30 days and achieve a 3.5% conversion rate from ad click to lead form submission. Would love your thoughts on whether these segments and KPIs feel realistic given what we can actually deliver.

Thanks for putting this together. I think the segments are solid, but I want to flag something on the KPIs. 150 leads in 30 days is ambitious given our current sales capacity. We've got three of us handling follow-up, and if each lead needs a technical consultation call, we're looking at roughly 50 calls per person per month. That's doable, but we need to make sure the lead quality is high enough that we're not chasing tire-kickers. Have you thought about a lead scoring model or qualification criteria we should bake into the form?

Good catch. I was thinking of that as a separate piece (part of T6, the lead workflow), but you're right—we should define qualification upfront. What if we add a budget range question and a timeline question to the form? That way we can route high-intent leads to you faster and maybe nurture the others with email first. Does that help with capacity?

That makes sense. One more thing—on the e-commerce segment, we should be clear about minimum order quantities and lead times. I've had conversations with some of those prospects before, and they often expect 2-week turnarounds. If we can't promise that, we need to set expectations early or we'll get a lot of inbound objections.

On the production side, I want to make sure we're aligned on what we can actually deliver. For the segments you mentioned, what's the typical catalog size and complexity? I need to understand the specs before I can confirm feasibility. Also, the value prop mentions 'print-quality'—we should define what that means in terms of color accuracy, paper stock options, and finishing. I'll be working on A3 (the creative and print spec guide) and I want to make sure it reflects what's actually possible.

Fair point. Let me add some detail to A1 on typical specs: we're thinking 24–48 page catalogs, full color, standard paper stocks (100–150 gsm), and basic finishing (saddle stitch or perfect bind). I'll also add a section on what we're NOT offering (e.g., no specialty finishes like foil or emboss in the first phase). That should help you scope T3 and give us a clearer picture of what's in scope.

I'm tracking the segments and specs. One question on the industrial suppliers segment—are we positioning this as a replacement for their existing printed materials, or as a new offering they can white-label or resell? That changes the messaging and the sales conversation quite a bit.

Good question. For now, we're positioning it as a replacement or upgrade to their current catalog process—so they're the end customer, not a reseller. We can explore white-label later if there's demand. I'll clarify that in A1.

Okay, that helps. So on the primary segments—e-commerce, industrial, professional services—I think those are solid. But I'd suggest we prioritize e-commerce and industrial for the launch, and treat professional services as a secondary segment we test with smaller budgets. The reason: e-commerce and industrial have clearer ROI stories and faster decision cycles. Professional services might need more nurturing.

I agree. Let me update A1 to reflect that prioritization. So to summarize where we are: primary segments are e-commerce and industrial suppliers, secondary is professional services. KPIs: 150 leads in 30 days, 3.5% conversion from ad to form. We'll add lead qualification questions to the form to help with routing. And we'll define print specs in A3 to make sure everything is feasible. Does that feel like a solid foundation to move forward?

I think so. I'll get started on A3 and T3 to map out the creative and print specs. I'll need to see some early creative mockups from you to validate feasibility, so we should probably sync on that in the next thread when you're working on the actual ad copy and landing page.

Sounds good. I'll also start drafting the FAQ and playbook outline (A4) based on these segments and value props. That way when we get to the sales enablement thread, we'll have something concrete to review.

threads.thread_goal: Lock channel mix, budget split, and launch timeline

messages.text: Alright, moving to the media plan. I've drafted A2 with a proposed channel mix and budget allocation. Here's the thinking: we have a total media budget of $45k. I'm proposing 40% to paid search (Google Ads, targeting high-intent keywords like 'custom printed catalogs'), 35% to LinkedIn ads (targeting decision-makers at our three segments), 15% to email nurture campaigns, and 10% contingency for optimization. The go-live date I'm targeting is 14 days from now, which gives us time to finalize creatives, get QA sign-off, and do a soft launch test. I've also outlined the tracking requirements in A7 so we can measure performance across channels. Thoughts?

The channel mix makes sense. Search and LinkedIn are the right plays for B2B. One question on the budget split: 40% to search feels high if we're still refining our value prop and messaging. What if we start with 30% search, bump LinkedIn to 40%, and keep the rest the same? That way we're leading with brand awareness and positioning, and search becomes the conversion play once we've warmed up the audience.

I see the logic, but I'm a bit concerned about search volume. If we go too light on search, we might miss high-intent traffic from people actively looking for catalog solutions. What if we split the difference: 35% search, 40% LinkedIn, 15% email, 10% contingency? That keeps search strong but gives LinkedIn more room to build awareness.

I think 35/40 works. From a sales perspective, I'd rather have a mix of high-intent search traffic and brand-aware LinkedIn leads. Both feed the funnel differently. On the timeline though—14 days is tight. We still need to finalize creatives, get them through QA with production, and do a test run. Can we push to day 16 or 17? That gives us a buffer for any issues that come up.

I agree on the timeline. 14 days is risky. I need time to review creatives against A3 specs, flag any issues, and get them corrected. Plus, we need to run through A5 (the QA checklist) before anything goes live. I'd say 16 days minimum, ideally 17 or 18.

Fair enough. Let me revise: launch date is day 17. That gives us 3 days for creative finalization and QA, which should be enough. I'll update A2 with the revised timeline and the 35/40 budget split. Does that work for everyone?

Day 17 works for me. One thing I want to make sure we're tracking: lead source attribution. With search and LinkedIn running simultaneously, we need to be able to tell which channel is driving the best-quality leads. I assume that's covered in A7?

Yes, A7 has the UTM structure and tracking events mapped out. We'll use utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign to differentiate between search and LinkedIn, and we'll track form submissions, lead quality scores, and downstream sales activity. I'll also set up a dashboard in our analytics tool so we can see performance in real time.
Good. And just to confirm—we're doing a soft launch on day 17, right? Not a full blast across all channels at once?

Yes, soft launch. We'll start with 50% of the planned budget on day 17, monitor for 24 hours, check for any tracking issues or creative problems, and then ramp to full budget on day 18. That way we catch any issues before they scale. I'll document the launch plan in T10.

threads.thread_goal: Validate creative concepts against print capabilities and finalize specs

messages.text: I've reviewed the early creative mockups that came through, and I need to flag a few things before we move forward. First, the color palette in the LinkedIn ad mockups is using RGB values that won't translate well to CMYK print. Second, the headline copy mentions 'unlimited color options,' but we're only offering standard 4-color process. Third, I haven't seen the landing page brief yet, so I can't validate those specs. I'm working on A3 (the creative and print spec guide) and A5 (the QA checklist), but I need clearer direction on what we're actually promising. Can we sync on this?

Good catches. I should have been more careful with the color specs. Let me clarify: we're offering standard 4-color process, no specialty finishes in phase one. I'll revise the copy to say 'vibrant full-color printing' instead of 'unlimited options.' On the landing page, I'm still drafting that, but I'll make sure it aligns with what you're documenting in A3. Can you send me the draft A3 so I can use it as a reference while I'm writing?

I'll have a draft of A3 ready by EOD tomorrow. It'll include color profiles (CMYK specs), paper stock options (100–150 gsm), binding options (saddle stitch and perfect bind), and a list of what we're NOT offering. I'll also include some sample mockups showing what the final product will look like. Once you see that, you can use it to write the landing page copy and make sure everything is consistent.

Perfect. I'll wait for A3 before I finalize the landing page brief. In the meantime, I'll revise the ad copy to remove the 'unlimited' language and stick to what we can actually deliver. I'll also make sure all customer-facing copy goes through compliance review before launch—that's part of T4.

One thing I want to make sure of: when we're talking to customers about lead times and delivery, are we promising anything specific? I want to make sure the sales team isn't overpromising on turnaround times.

Good question. From a production standpoint, once we receive final files and approval, we can turn around a standard 24–48 page catalog in 10–15 business days. That includes printing, binding, and QC. But that assumes the customer provides files in the right format and approves proofs quickly. I'll document this in A3 so it's clear to the sales team and marketing.
10–15 business days is good. That's competitive. I'll make sure that's in the FAQ and sales playbook (A4) so we're all saying the same thing.

Okay, so to lock this down: we're promising 4-color process, standard paper stocks, saddle stitch or perfect bind, 10–15 business day turnaround. No specialty finishes in phase one. All copy will reflect this, and it'll be documented in A3. Once A3 is finalized, I'll use it to write the landing page brief and make sure everything is consistent. Then we'll run through A5 (the QA checklist) before launch. Does that cover it?

Yes, that covers it. I'll have A3 and a draft of A5 ready by EOD tomorrow. Once you finalize the landing page and ad copy, send them my way and I'll do a full review against A3 and A5 to make sure everything is print-safe and accurate.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize sales playbook, lead workflow, and training approach

messages.text: I've put together a draft of the sales playbook (A4) and the lead workflow (A6). The playbook includes a pitch outline, objection handling for common concerns (price, turnaround, customization limits), and a process flow for moving a lead from inquiry to proposal. The workflow document outlines how leads come in from the form, how we route them based on segment and budget, and what the SLAs are for follow-up. I've set response time targets at 2 hours for high-priority leads (budget >$10k) and 24 hours for standard leads. I'd like feedback from the team, especially on whether these SLAs are realistic and whether the pitch messaging aligns with what marketing is saying.

Good work. The SLAs look reasonable. 2 hours for high-priority is tight but doable if we're monitoring the inbox. One thing I'd add to the playbook: a section on how to handle requests for features we don't offer yet (like specialty finishes). We need a consistent way to say 'not now, but we're exploring it' without losing the deal. Also, I want to make sure the pitch emphasizes the customization angle—that's our differentiator versus generic catalog services.

I agree on the customization angle. And on the SLAs, I'd suggest we also track response time by segment. E-commerce leads might need faster response than industrial, just because of how they operate. Can we build that into A6?

Good idea. I'll add segment-specific SLAs to A6. E-commerce: 1.5 hours for high-priority, 12 hours for standard. Industrial: 2 hours for high-priority, 24 hours for standard. Professional services: 4 hours for high-priority, 48 hours for standard. Does that feel right?

That makes sense from a sales perspective. From marketing, I want to make sure the playbook messaging aligns with what we're saying in ads and the landing page. Can you send me the draft pitch outline so I can review it against the value props we locked in earlier?

I'll send you the pitch outline by EOD today. It's built around three main points: (1) customization—we work with you to design catalogs that match your brand, (2) quality—full-color, professional printing with fast turnaround, (3) efficiency—cost-effective at scale. Does that align with what you're messaging?

Yes, that aligns well. I'm using 'customization,' 'quality,' and 'efficiency' as the three pillars in the landing page and ad copy too. Good. Now, on training—when do you want to run the sales enablement session (T9)? We should do it after the playbook is finalized but before launch, so everyone's on the same page.

I'd suggest we do the training on day 15 or 16, so it's fresh in everyone's mind before launch on day 17. That gives us time to address any questions and make last-minute adjustments to the playbook if needed.

Day 15 works for me. I'll have the final playbook and workflow ready by day 14, so we have time to review before the training. I'll also prepare a quick reference guide (one-pager) that the team can keep handy during the first few days of launch.

Perfect. So to summarize: A4 (playbook) and A6 (workflow) finalized by day 14, training on day 15, launch on day 17. The playbook includes pitch outline, objection handling, and customization messaging. The workflow has segment-specific SLAs and lead routing rules. Does everyone agree this is locked?
Locked. I'll get the final versions ready by day 14.

threads.thread_goal: Review early performance, customer feedback, and next optimizations

messages.text: We're 72 hours post-launch and I wanted to share the initial performance snapshot. A7 (tracking and reporting) is showing us good data. Here's what we're seeing: 187 total clicks across search and LinkedIn, 42 form submissions (22.5% conversion rate—above our 3.5% target), 18 qualified leads (high-priority based on budget and timeline), 8 leads already in sales conversations. Search is outperforming LinkedIn on conversion (28% vs 18%), but LinkedIn is driving more volume. Cost per lead is tracking at $214, which is within budget. No major tracking issues or broken links. I'm drafting the post-launch report (A8) and I'd like input from sales on lead quality and from production on any feasibility concerns that have come up.

Great start. From the sales side, the lead quality is solid. Of the 18 qualified leads, I'd say 15 are genuinely interested and have realistic budgets. The other 3 are still exploring, but they're not tire-kickers. Response times are holding up—we're hitting the 2-hour SLA for high-priority leads about 80% of the time. One thing I'm noticing: a lot of leads are asking about timeline flexibility. Some want faster turnaround than our 10–15 day standard. We're handling it okay with the playbook, but it might be worth testing a 'rush' option in the next phase.

I'm seeing the same thing on timeline requests. A few leads have asked if we can do 5–7 day turnaround for a premium. I haven't committed to anything, but it's worth exploring. From a production standpoint, is that feasible?

5–7 days is tight, but maybe doable for smaller jobs (under 32 pages) if we prioritize them. But that would require some process changes on our end and might impact our standard turnaround for other jobs. I'd say let's not promise it yet, but we can explore it as a future offering. For now, I'd stick with the 10–15 day standard and position it as competitive.
Agreed. We can mention in follow-up conversations that we're exploring expedited options, but we shouldn't promise them yet. That keeps the door open without overcommitting.
Good. I'll note that in A8 as a future optimization. On the creative side, are there any issues with the ads or landing page that have come up?

No major issues. The creatives are holding up well. One small thing: the LinkedIn ad copy mentions 'unlimited customization,' which is a bit of an overstatement. We should tighten that language to 'extensive customization options' or something similar. But that's a minor tweak for the next iteration.
I'll make that adjustment in the next ad refresh. Anything else from production or sales that should go in the report?

One more thing: I'd like to start collecting customer feedback from the first few deals that close. That's part of T11. I'm planning to do brief follow-up calls with customers after they receive their catalogs to understand what worked and what didn't. That feedback will be valuable for the final report.

Perfect. That's exactly what we need for T11 and T12. I'll incorporate that feedback into A8 once you have it. So here's the plan: I'll finalize A8 with the 72-hour snapshot and initial learnings by day 20. You'll collect customer feedback over the next week or so, and we'll do a final report by day 21 with all the data. Sound good?
Sounds good. I'll also start documenting any technical issues or edge cases that come up during the first week, so we can address them in the next phase.

Great. So to recap: we're tracking well against our KPIs, lead quality is solid, and we've identified a few optimization opportunities (rush turnaround, language tweaks, customer feedback). I'll have the full post-launch report ready by day 21 with recommendations for the next phase. Thanks everyone for the solid execution.
